blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text: Immunity is the body's ability to resist harmful microorganisms, involving both specific and non-specific defense mechanisms. Vaccination stimulates the immune system to develop adaptive immunity to a pathogen.

blocks.title: Acquired Immunity
blocks.text:
Types of Lymphocytes :-

  • B-lymphocytes: Antibodies are proteins produced by B cells to neutralize pathogens. They consist of two light chains and two heavy chains (H₂L₂). Key antibody 5 types include IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD and IgG. This antibody-mediated response is called the humoral immune response.
  • T-lymphocytes: These cells do not secrete antibodies but help B-cells in antibody production. T-cells also mediate the cell-mediated immune response (CMI), which is crucial for the body’s ability to reject foreign tissues or organs (e.g., during grafts or transplants).
Organ Transplantation :-

During organ transplants, tissue matching and blood group matching are essential to prevent rejection. Even with matching, patients must take immunosuppressants to reduce the risk of the body recognizing the transplant as "non-self" and rejecting it, a process controlled by the cell-mediated immune response.

blocks.title: Vaccination
blocks.text:
Vaccination is the process of artificially providing acquired immunity to a specific infection or disease by administering a vaccine. It is used as a prophylactic measure to prevent infections.

Principle of Vaccination :-

  • A vaccine is a preparation containing weakened or inactivated pathogens, pathogenic exotoxins (with the toxicity removed), or antigenic proteins of the pathogen.
  • Vaccines can be administered orally or via injection to stimulate immunity against that pathogen.

blocks.title: Auto Immunity
blocks.text: Definition: Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own cells, leading to tissue damage.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing Immunity Types: Innate is non-specific; adaptive is specific.
  • Misidentifying Vaccine Types: Clarity between live attenuated and inactivated vaccines.
  • Overlooking Memory: Immunological memory is key in vaccine effectiveness.
  • Avoiding Over-simplification: Recognize specific roles of B cells vs. T cells.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
Which immune response / immunity is mainly responsible for graft rejection ?

(1) Cell-mediated

(2) Humoral

(3) Antibody mediated

(4) All of the above
blocks.answer:
Ans- 1

The immune system can differentiate between "self" and "nonself". During a transplant, the recipient's immune system recognizes the transplanted tissue or organ as foreign and launches a cell-mediated immune response. This response involves T cells, which identify and attack foreign tissues.

modules.name: AIDS and Its Impact on the Immune System

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text: AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) is a chronic condition caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which damages the immune system by targeting T cells, leading to vulnerability to opportunistic infections.

blocks.title: Key Concepts
blocks.text:
HIV Structure :-

  • Retrovirus with RNA genome
  • Reverse transcriptase enzyme

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing HIV with AIDS: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the condition.
  • Misunderstanding Transmission Routes: Not spread through casual contact, air, water, insect bites.
  • Ignoring Early Treatment: Delayed ART can accelerate AIDS progression.

blocks.title: HIV Question 1
blocks.question:
In which blood corpuscles, the HIV undergoes replication and produces progeny viruses ?

(1) B-lymphocytes

(2) Basophils

(3) Eosinophils

(4) Helper T- Lymphocytes
blocks.answer:
Answer - 4.

HIV enters into helper T-lymphocytes in which they reverse transcribe DNA and then replicate to produce progeny .

(4) HIV is enveloped virus that contains two identical molecules of single- stranded RNA and two molecules of reverse transcriptase.

blocks.text: Cancer involves uncontrolled cell division due to mutations in genes regulating cell growth, transforming normal cells into tumor cells and leading to malignant growths affecting various organs.

blocks.title: Point To Remember
blocks.text:
Important Nomenclatures:

  • Metastasis: Spread of cancer cells from the original site to other parts of the body.
  • Benign vs. Malignant: Benign tumors are non-cancerous; malignant tumors invade surrounding tissues.

blocks.title: Mechanism of Cancer
blocks.text:
• In our body, cell growth and differentiation is highly controlled and regulated. In cancer cells, there is breakdown of these regulatory mechanisms.
    • Tumour suppressor genes inhibit cellular proliferation.

Several genes called cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto oncogenes have been identified in normal cells which, when activated under certain conditions, could lead to oncogenic transformation of the cells.

${\text {Normal cell}} \xrightarrow[\text { Induced by Carcinogens }]{\text { Oncogenic Transformation }} {\text {Tumour cell}}$

$$

blocks.title: Tumor Promoters
blocks.text: • Agents that promote the proliferation of cells, which have already undergone genetic alternations responsible for oncogenic transformation. These agents are called tumor promoters. e.g. Some growth factors and hormones.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusion between Benign and Malignant: Remember, benign tumors do not spread; malignant ones do.
  • Misinterpretation of Imaging Results: Understand each imaging technique's purpose and limitations.
  • Overlooking Lifestyle Factors: Recognize lifestyle's significant impact on cancer risk reduction.

modules.name: Drug and Alochol Abuse : Effects and Prevention

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Substance abuse involves harmful use such as alcohol and drugs, potentially leading to dependency and adverse health effects. Prevention aims to reduce availability and demand for these substances.

rows: Alcohol, Opioids (e.g., heroin), Cannabis, Nicotine, Cocaine, Amphetamines,
Physical:Liver damage (alcohol), respiratory issues (smoking), cardiovascular problems (cocaine)
Education and Awareness: Informing about dangers and consequences
Regulation and Law Enforcement: Restricting access, legal age limits
Rehabilitation Programs: Offering therapy and support for recovery
Community and Family Support: Encouraging healthy lifestyle choices
Dependence: Habitual use leading to withdrawal symptoms
Tolerance: Need for increased amounts to achieve desired effect

blocks.title: Alcohol Abuse
blocks.text:
Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol) Consumption and Effects

Types of Beverages:
    • Fermented (low alcohol): Beer, wine.

• Distilled (high alcohol): Brandy, rum, whisky, gin.

• Absorption: Rapidly absorbed in the stomach and enters the bloodstream within minutes.

• Metabolism: Alcohol converts to acetaldehyde, a more toxic substance.

Effects of Alcohol Abuse

  • Liver Damage
  • Brain Impact
  • Blood Sugar
  • Immune System
  • Reproductive Health
  • Foetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS)
  • Digestive Issues

blocks.title: Tobacco Abuse
blocks.text:
Tobacco Use and Health Risks:-

• Forms of Use: Smoked, chewed, or used as snuff.

• Key Chemical: Contains nicotine, an alkaloid.

Health Risks of Smoking:-

• Increased CO in Blood

• Gateway to Hard Drugs

Diseases Associated with Smoking:-

  • Cancers
  • Respiratory Diseases
  • Heart Disease
  • Other Risks

blocks.title: Adolescence and Drug/Alcohol Abuse
blocks.text:
Adolescence Overview

• Definition: A period and process of transition from childhood to adulthood (ages 12-18).
    • Development: Involves maturation in attitudes, beliefs, and readiness for societal roles.
    • Characteristics: Biological and behavioural changes; a vulnerable phase for mental and psychological growth.

Influence of Friends on Substance Use

• Peer Influence: Friends can strongly impact choices to try alcohol, tobacco, or drugs.
    • Prevention:
Build self-confidence and assertiveness.
Develop awareness of risks.
Surround oneself with supportive, positive influences.

Motivations for Substance Use in Adolescents

Initial Triggers:

• Curiosity and desire for adventure.

• Experimentation and the perception that it’s “cool” (influenced by media).

Long-Term Factors:

• Escape from personal issues or stress.
    • Academic or family pressures.
    • Peer pressure and lack of family support.
